doc.title: Lisa Parrott interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 22, 2021

title: What music means: joy of playing for an audience
summary: On first playing for an audience after the pandemic and wanting melody and love to reach listeners.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Well you’re directing me to a vaguely formed question and also connected with I believe this is a quote from Ornette Coleman, “There is a music that has the quality to preserve life.” And I wonder two things: what does music — what can music mean? And what do you hope an audience listening to your music will get out of it?

First of all I’m tearing up because I relate so much to this, and especially since I’ve just come off the back of barely playing with anybody for almost a year and a half. And before I left on this trip, in May I finally played some duets at a little art gallery in Brooklyn with my friend Jamie Fox. And we’re both vaccinated so we’ve both been getting together. He was the first person I didn’t wear a mask around, we were both like can we do this? I think we can. And then we actually played a gig for about ten people in a loft gallery that opened up into the side of a street which was a great little Brooklyn gig, but I will never forget that feeling. I was very surprised by it, that it had been a very long time since I felt that much joy in playing. So it was a really wonderful feeling to realize, you know, you know in your head this means a lot to you, you’ve made a career out of this, but at the same time oh wow there are certain things you can’t do if you’re not playing for an audience. I mean there are certain things you just don’t sort of play. You know rehearsing is not anything like performing. It really isn’t. Because we went to places, musical places, that we hadn’t been to and we just had massive smiles on our faces and it was so joyful. And I just want to really remember that feeling of how important it is, and the audience were feeling it too. That was very obvious as well. Everyone was just very very happy for the experience but also it was wonderful to have a dedicated listening audience. So that sort of feeling that I was trying to describe is what I aim for and I want to try to get each time I play where there’s such a deep connection

with the musicians that the audience cannot help but be brought into that and also taken along for that experience. And I would hope that, I suppose if my Dad can come to one of my gigs where I’m playing heavy harmolodics [gestures air quotes] — I’m saying that in embedded commas because like some of it, my, was it two years ago or maybe three years ago, but one of my last times I was out here playing gigs Harry, the bass player, came and he was not expecting to like my music. And he was fascinated. He was like, “I never listen to music like that but I love that. Why?” He was like, “Come over for wine and sourdough bread. And I’m fascinated, why did I like it?” And I said, “It’s about melody” because I’m always coming from melody. So no matter how chaotic it might sort of sound if you just pick apart the pieces I always want to try to get a high form of, it’s always coming from a loving, melodic place. I feel like melody is love, I really do. Yeah. So that’s what I would hope an audience gets out of it. Like, love.
And I’m tearing up because you know because of what’s happened this year you know.
